Series::histogram¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

std::pair<Series, Series> Series::histogram(std::int64_t bins = 100,
                                            bool density = false) const
std::pair<Series, Series> Series::histogram(std::int64_t bins,
                                            double lo, double hi,
                                            bool density = false) const

What It Does¶

Divides a value range into bins equal-width buckets and counts how many elements fall in each, returning both the counts and the bucket boundaries.

The result is a std::pair<Series, Series>:

  • .first is hist — a length-bins float64 series. Bin i holds the number of elements in the half-open interval [edges[i], edges[i + 1]), except the final bin, whose upper edge is inclusive so the maximum value is not lost.

  • .second is bin_edges — a length-bins + 1 float64 series, the evenly spaced boundaries.

Returning the edges is the whole reason this is a separate call from histc(), which returns only the counts. You almost always need the edges: to label an axis, to find a bin’s centre, to interpret the shape. Bind them together:

auto [hist, edges] = data.histogram(20);

The range is either given (histogram(bins, lo, hi)) or inferred — the default form spans the finite [min, max] of the data. Values outside the range, and any NaN / inf, are simply not counted.

Set density = true to normalize: each count becomes count / (total * bin_width), so the bars integrate to 1 (sum(hist * bin_width) == 1) and you have a probability density estimate rather than raw tallies.

Parameters¶

bins (std::int64_t): the number of equal-width buckets. Must be > 0. Default 100.

lo, hi (double): the inclusive lower and upper bounds of the range. When omitted, the range is the finite minimum and maximum of the data. A degenerate range (hi <= lo, which also happens when every value is equal) is widened to [lo - 0.5, hi + 0.5].

density (bool): when true, return a probability density instead of counts. Default false.

Returns¶

std::pair<Series, Series> {hist, bin_edges}. hist has length bins; bin_edges has length bins + 1. Both are float64 and on the input’s platform. hist is float64 even for integer input and even without density.

Gradient¶

histogram() is a bucketing operation with locally constant output. It is not differentiable.

Examples¶

Example 1. Seven values into four bins over [0, 3].

auto [hist, edges] =
    pluss::make_series({0.0, 1.0, 1.0, 2.0, 2.0, 2.0, 3.0}).histogram(4);

std::cout << "hist  = " << hist;
std::cout << "edges = " << edges;

Output¶

hist  = pluss::Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 2, 3, 1]edges = pluss::Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0.75, 1.5, 2.25, 3]

Bin 0 is [0, 0.75) and catches the single 0. Bin 1 [0.75, 1.5) catches the two 1s. Bin 2 [1.5, 2.25) catches the three 2s. Bin 3 [2.25, 3] catches the 3 — the top edge is inclusive.

Example 2. The inclusive top edge, shown directly: 1.0 is the maximum and it lands in the last bin rather than falling off the end.

auto [hist, edges] = pluss::make_series({0.0, 0.5, 1.0}).histogram(2);

std::cout << "hist  = " << hist;
std::cout << "edges = " << edges;

Output¶

hist  = pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 2]edges = pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0.5, 1]

Bin 0 [0, 0.5) gets {0}; bin 1 [0.5, 1] gets {0.5, 1}.

Example 3. An explicit range clips: values below lo or above hi are dropped, not clamped into the edge bins.

auto [hist, edges] =
    pluss::make_series({-5.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 9.0}).histogram(2, 0.0, 2.0);

std::cout << "hist  = " << hist;
std::cout << "edges = " << edges;

Output¶

hist  = pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 2]edges = pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 1, 2]

-5 and 9 are outside [0, 2] and contribute nothing. Only {0} and {1, 2} are counted.

Example 4. density = true rescales so the histogram integrates to 1.

auto [hist, edges] =
    pluss::make_series({0.0, 1.0, 1.0, 2.0, 2.0, 2.0, 3.0}).histogram(4, true);

std::cout << "hist = " << hist;

const double width = 3.0 / 4.0;  // (hi - lo) / bins
pluss::series::print(std::cout, hist.mul(width).sum());

Output¶

hist = pluss::Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0.19047619, 0.38095238, 0.57142857, 0.19047619]Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=1.0000

Each bar is count / (7 * 0.75), and sum(hist * width) is exactly 1.

Example 5. inf and NaN fall outside every finite bin and are ignored.

auto [hist, edges] = pluss::make_series({
    0.5, 1.5,
    std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity(),
    std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN(),
    2.5,
}).histogram(3, 0.0, 3.0);

std::cout << "hist  = " << hist;
std::cout << "edges = " << edges;

Output¶

hist  = pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 1, 1]edges = pluss::Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 1, 2, 3]

Only 0.5, 1.5, and 2.5 are counted, one per bin.

Example 6. When every value is identical the inferred range is degenerate, so it is widened by 0.5 on each side.

auto [hist, edges] = pluss::make_series({4.0, 4.0, 4.0}).histogram(2);

std::cout << "hist  = " << hist;
std::cout << "edges = " << edges;

Output¶

hist  = pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 3]edges = pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[3.5, 4, 4.5]

The range becomes [3.5, 4.5]; all three 4s land in the upper bin [4, 4.5].

Example 7. A multi-dimensional input is flattened before binning.

auto [hist, edges] =
    pluss::make_series({{0.0, 1.0}, {2.0, 3.0}}).histogram(3, 0.0, 3.0);

std::cout << "hist  = " << hist;
std::cout << "edges = " << edges;

Output¶

hist  = pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 1, 2]edges = pluss::Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 1, 2, 3]

Example 8. Contrast with histc(), which returns only the counts, as int64, with no edges.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({0.0, 1.0, 1.0, 2.0, 2.0, 2.0, 3.0})
                 .histc(4, 0.0, 3.0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 2, 3, 1]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • hist is float64, always — even for integer input and even without density. Cast it if you need integer counts, or use histc().

  • bin_edges has bins + 1 entries, one more than hist.

  • Values < lo or > hi are dropped, not clamped into the boundary bins.

  • NaN and inf are never counted.

  • The inferred range spans the finite data; a lone inf does not stretch it.

  • bins must be > 0; bins = 0 raises.

  • Not differentiable.

  • For a tally of repeated integer labels (not a value range), use bincount().

Summary¶

histogram() buckets values into equal-width bins and returns both parts:

  • std::pair<Series, Series> = {hist (float64, length bins), bin_edges (float64, length bins + 1)} — bind as auto [h, e] = ...

  • range is given, or the finite [min, max]; out-of-range and non-finite values are dropped

  • the top edge is inclusive

  • density = true gives a probability density (sum(hist * width) == 1)

  • not differentiable

See Also¶

  • Series::histc: the same binning, counts only, int64, no edges.

  • Series::bincount: tally non-negative integer values directly, one bin per integer.

  • Series::aminmax: the [min, max] the default range comes from.

  • Series::quantile: summarize a distribution by percentile instead of by bin.
